content: The immature epidermal barrier in preterm infants can break down, allowing microorganisms to enter and potentially cause invasive infections. These infections are a significant cause of both mortality and morbidity in this vulnerable population. The application of topical emollients, such as ointments, creams, or oils, has been proposed as a method to enhance skin integrity and barrier function, potentially reducing the risk of such infections. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the effects of topical emollients on the risk of invasive infection and mortality in preterm infants. The review included randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials that assessed the prophylactic use of emollients in this population. The search for relevant studies was performed using CENTRAL via the Cochrane Register of Studies and MEDLINE, with the last update on January 8, 2021. Standard Cochrane Neonatal methods were employed for data collection and analysis, including the use of risk ratios (RR), risk differences (RD), and mean differences to synthesize effect estimates. The GRADE approach was used to assess the certainty of the evidence. A total of 22 trials involving 5578 preterm infants were included in the review. The main sources of potential bias in these studies were unclear methods for random sequence generation and allocation concealment in about half of the trials, as well as the lack of masking of parents, caregivers, clinicians, and investigators in all trials. Eight trials, including 2086 infants, investigated the use of topical ointments or creams. Most of these studies were conducted in high-income countries and involved very preterm infants cared for in healthcare facilities. Meta-analyses suggested that the use of topical ointments or creams may have little to no effect on the risk of invasive infection (RR 1.13, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.31; low certainty evidence) or mortality (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.08; low certainty evidence). Fifteen trials, involving 3492 infants, examined the effects of topical plant or vegetable oils. Most of these studies were conducted in lowor middle-income countries, primarily in healthcare facilities, with one large community-based trial (2249 infants) conducted in a rural area of India. Meta-analyses suggested that topical oils may reduce the risk of invasive infection (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.96; I² = 52%; low certainty evidence) but have little to no effect on mortality (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.08; I² = 3%; low certainty evidence). One trial conducted in Bangladesh compared the use of petroleum-based ointment versus sunflower seed oil in 316 very preterm infants. The results indicated little to no effect on invasive infection (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.46; low certainty evidence), but the use of ointment may slightly reduce mortality (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.68 to 0.98; RD -0.12, 95% CI -0.23 to -0.01; number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome = 8, 95% CI 4 to 100; low certainty evidence). Another trial conducted in India involved 64 preterm infants with birth weights between 1500 g and 2000 g and compared the use of coconut oil versus mineral oil. This study reported no episodes of invasive infection or death in either group, but the certainty of the evidence was very low. In conclusion, the evidence regarding the effects of emollient therapy on invasive infection and mortality in preterm infants is of low certainty. However, given that these interventions are generally inexpensive, widely available, and acceptable, further high-quality randomized controlled trials, particularly in healthcare facilities and community settings in lowor middle-income countries, may be warranted.
